lede: Washington's role in the region's civil–military relations no longer runs through aid tables alone. Grants, officer training, basing, detention and, since 2025, direct military action form one continuum of leverage, and this page reads them together.

caribbean.title: The Caribbean campaign
intro: Since January 2025 the United States has moved from aid conditionality and multilateral frameworks to direct coercion in the Caribbean basin: a terrorist frame for criminal groups, lethal strikes at sea, a forward military build-up, and in January 2026 the capture of Venezuela's president in Caracas. The Caribbean, long a secondary theatre beneath the Andean and Central American corridors, became the hemisphere's most active zone of US military engagement.

timeline.title: Guantánamo opened to migrants
timeline.text: A presidential memorandum ordered the naval base's migrant operations center expanded to hold up to 30,000 people. In practice it held far fewer: about 500 had passed through by June 2025, usually a few dozen at a time.

timeline.title: Cartels designated as terrorists
timeline.text: Eight Latin American groups were designated foreign terrorist organizations on 20 February; the list reached 21 by September 2026.

timeline.title: Deportees sent to El Salvador's CECOT
timeline.text: More than 200 Venezuelans accused of belonging to Tren de Aragua were flown to the CECOT mega-prison under the Alien Enemies Act. In July 2025 they were returned to Venezuela in an exchange for ten detained Americans; Caracas put the number at 252.

timeline.title: Strikes at sea begin
timeline.text: The US military began striking boats it said were carrying drugs, first in the Caribbean and later in the eastern Pacific. The campaign was named Operation Southern Spear in November. By 4 October 2026 at least 238 people had been killed in at least 79 strikes. The Pentagon has not shown that those on board were trafficking drugs.

timeline.title: Roosevelt Roads reopened
timeline.text: The former naval station in Puerto Rico, closed since 2004, was reactivated for F-35B fighters, drones and maritime patrol aircraft. More than 10,000 US personnel were in the Southern Command area by November, with the carrier USS Gerald R. Ford on its way.

timeline.title: A new force for Haiti
timeline.text: The UN Security Council authorized a 5,500-strong Gang Suppression Force with powers of arrest to replace the Kenyan-led mission. By June 2026 fewer than 1,000 troops had arrived.

timeline.title: Ecuador rejects foreign bases
timeline.text: Voters turned down President Noboa's proposal to allow foreign military bases, 60.6% to 39.4%, a setback for plans to bring US forces back to Manta.

timeline.title: Cartel de los Soles designated
timeline.text: The State Department designated the network it says is headed by Nicolás Maduro a foreign terrorist organization, effective 24 November.

timeline.title: Operation Absolute Resolve
timeline.text: US forces captured Nicolás Maduro in Caracas on 3 January. He was arraigned in New York on narco-terrorism charges on 5 January, and Delcy Rodríguez became acting president.

assessment: The 2025–26 operations mark a structural shift in US posture in the hemisphere, from institution-building and aid conditionality towards direct coercion and transactional bilateral deals. The capture of a sitting head of state in his own capital has no post-1989 precedent. For civil–military relations the lessons are uneven: armed forces loyal to a sanctioned leader learned that loyalty does not buy sovereignty; smaller Caribbean militaries now plan for the possibility of US direct action; and the CECOT arrangement showed Washington willing to finance detention outside the inter-American human-rights system. SENTINEL's assessment is that the net effect on regional civil–military norms is destabilizing: it may shorten some authoritarian tenures while normalizing extralegal executive force.

access.title: The access network
access.note: Not only bases: a regional network that links detention, surveillance flights, logistics, counternarcotics patrols and crisis response across the Caribbean basin and northern South America.

channels_note: Military and counternarcotics money reaches the region through distinct funding accounts, each with its own legal authority and oversight. International Narcotics Control and Law Enforcement (INCLE) and Foreign Military Financing (FMF) are the largest. International Military Education and Training (IMET) is small but reaches almost every country, and is the channel most studied for its effect on officers' attitudes to civilian control. Defense Department accounts, among them the Section 333 train-and-equip authority, let the Pentagon fund partner forces directly, without a State Department lead, and are reported with a longer lag.
